# Quantifiable Metrics for Software Upgrade Validation in Operator-Deployed Kubernetes Platforms

## Introduction

This document catalogs the quantifiable metrics available for validating Kubernetes platform and operator upgrades. It covers 8 dimensions across the upgrade lifecycle: data integrity, functional testing, duration, rollback, workload continuity, version skip support, API compatibility, and operator lifecycle mechanics.

**Scope:** Operator-deployed Kubernetes platforms (OpenShift, vanilla K8s with operators, managed services). Broader infrastructure projects (PostgreSQL, etcd, CockroachDB) are included where their metrics inform Kubernetes upgrade validation patterns.

**Key framing adjustments:**
1. Many projects use binary pass/fail gates rather than continuous metrics. The metric taxonomy in each section distinguishes these.
2. Operator-measurable metrics (what you can monitor in your cluster) are distinguished from vendor-measurable metrics (what the platform vendor tests in CI).
3. Rolling/continuous upgrade patterns receive explicit coverage alongside point-in-time upgrades.

**Methodology:** 75 sources visited in-session via WebSearch and WebFetch. 16 research agents (8 discovery + 8 counter-discovery) ran in parallel, followed by multi-engine search augmentation (DuckDuckGo). Two independent review agents will audit the output. See [citations.md](citations.md) for all sources.

## Metric Taxonomy

Metrics fall into three categories:

| Category | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Continuous numeric** | A number that changes over time and can be tracked, trended, and alerted on | `kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total`, API endpoint coverage % |
| **Binary pass/fail** | A gate that either passes or doesn't | CNCF conformance (100% required), CSV phase (Succeeded or not) |
| **Threshold-based** | A continuous metric with a defined acceptable range | OpenShift 95% test pass rate, Flagger 99% success rate |

Most upgrade validation in the Kubernetes ecosystem uses **binary pass/fail** gates. Continuous numeric metrics exist but lack ecosystem-wide thresholds — organizations must define their own acceptable ranges.

## 1. Data Integrity Verification

**Summary:** Database projects provide the most quantitative metrics in this research. etcd, PostgreSQL, and CockroachDB all expose continuous checksums or integrity counts, while AWS DMS provides per-minute validation rates. The counter-perspective is critical: checksums have known coverage gaps, and silent failures have occurred in production.

| System | Primary Metric | Type | Coverage Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| etcd | Compacted hash check (every 1 min) [1] | Binary pass/fail | Does not handle slow followers |
| etcd | Latest revision hash (every ~2 hrs) [1] | Binary pass/fail | "High performance cost" |
| PostgreSQL | `checksum_failures` counter [3] | Continuous numeric | No temp files, no internal structures [2] [10] |
| CockroachDB | Underreplicated ranges (target: 0) [5] | Continuous gauge | Migration-specific only |
| CockroachDB | MOLT Verify row counts [4] | Continuous per table | 7 output metrics per table |
| AWS DMS | 7 CloudWatch metrics/min [6] | Continuous numeric | Stops at 10,000 failures |

**Critical counter-evidence:** etcd v3.5 data inconsistency postmortem [7], CockroachDB v22.1.0 silent changefeed failure with zero error logging [9], PostgreSQL checksums absent from SLRU files and visibility map [10]. Over 80% of data migration projects exceed time or budget (Tier 2 source, unverified).

See [references/data-integrity.md](references/data-integrity.md) for full details.

## 2. Functional Smoke Coverage

**Summary:** The CNCF conformance program requires 100% pass rate [13], but the conformance suite is only ~5-6% of the total e2e test suite [12] [16]. OpenShift is the only platform with published numeric CI thresholds (95%/70%/<1%). No industry standard exists for "what percentage of tests should run post-upgrade."

| Platform | Metric | Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| CNCF Conformance | Pass rate | 100% required, zero skips [13] |
| OpenShift (new tests) | Pass rate | 95% [14] |
| OpenShift (informing jobs) | Pass rate | 70% after one sprint [14] |
| OpenShift (blocking jobs) | Flake rate | <1% [14] |
| OpenShift (regression) | Statistical test | Fisher's Exact for multi-day patterns [14] |
| Operator SDK Scorecard | 6 tests | Binary pass/fail [17] |

Conformance test growth: 177 (v1.11) → 215 (v1.16) → 278 (v1.17) → 404 (v1.21-v1.27), representing ~5-6% of the total e2e suite (5.6% at v1.27) [12] [16]. API endpoint coverage: 11% (2018) → ~94% (v1.25) [15]. K8s 1.32 was the first release to achieve 100% conformance coverage [18].

**Critical counter-evidence:** 25%+ failure rates in K8s 1.5→1.7 upgrade test jobs [19]. Conformance tests cover "core of Kubernetes functionality" [12] only — implementation-specific features are explicitly excluded. The question "what percentage is standard" may itself be flawed; practitioners focus on risk-based critical-path testing rather than coverage percentages.

See [references/functional-smoke-coverage.md](references/functional-smoke-coverage.md) for full details.

## 3. Upgrade Duration SLOs

**Summary:** No platform publishes P95/P99 upgrade duration targets. OpenShift provides the only deterministic formula. Cloud providers converge on 4-hour maintenance windows without formal duration SLOs.

| Platform | Control Plane | Per Node | Formula/Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| OpenShift | 60-120 min (CVO) [20] | 5+ min (MCO) [20] | `CVO + (iterations × MCO)` |
| AKS | 5-15 min [21] | Drain 30 min (15-120 configurable) [22] | 4-hr maintenance window [23] |
| EKS | "several minutes" [24] | — | No specific number published |
| GKE | Not specified [25] | "up to a few hours" [25] | 99.5-99.95% uptime SLO, NOT upgrade SLO [26] |

Environmental variation makes universal SLOs impractical: bare metal reboots take 15+ minutes vs 1-2 minutes in cloud — a 7-15x difference from a single variable [20] [27]. PDB-induced delays can add up to 1 hour per node [25].

**Critical counter-evidence:** "Rushing upgrades leads to outages" (multiple Tier 2-3 sources). A single minor upgrade across 3 regions consumes 4-6 weeks engineering effort [70]. OpenShift IBU reduces telco upgrade time to ~15-20 minutes [28] — a purpose-built exception that proves the general case lacks targets.

See [references/upgrade-duration-slos.md](references/upgrade-duration-slos.md) for full details.

## 4. Rollback Success Rate

**Summary:** Rollback is not measured as a success rate. DORA metrics count rollbacks as deployment failures (Change Failure Rate ~5% for top performers [69]). Kubernetes control plane was forward-only until v1.33 [29]. Progressive delivery tools measure *when to trigger* rollback, not *whether rollback succeeds*.

| Platform | Rollback Support | Metric |
|---|---|---|
| K8s 1.33+ | Two-step rollback (KEP-4330) [29] | Binary (step 1 rollbackable, step 2 not) |
| OpenShift 4.x | Not supported [32] | Recovery via etcd backup/restore |
| OLM operators | Not supported [33] | Fix-forward recommended |
| GKE | Auto-rollback for failed CP upgrades | Binary |
| Flagger | Automated at 99% success threshold [31] | 10 failed checks before trigger |
| DORA | Change Failure Rate [30] | ~5% for elite performers [69] |

**Critical counter-evidence:** Rollback is often technically impossible due to destructive migrations, CRD schema changes, and irreversible state [32] [33]. The Rollback Paradox: rollback is most needed in catastrophic failures, which are exactly the cases where it cannot work.

See [references/rollback-success-rate.md](references/rollback-success-rate.md) for full details.

## 5. Stateful Workload Continuity

**Summary:** kube-state-metrics provides STABLE Prometheus metrics for PDB enforcement and pod restart tracking. However, PDBs only apply to voluntary disruptions via the eviction API, and restart count is a cumulative counter with known measurement limitations.

| Metric | Type | Stability | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kube_poddisruptionbudget_status_pod_disruptions_allowed` [37] | Gauge | STABLE | Disruptions currently permitted |
| `kube_poddisruptionbudget_status_current_healthy` [37] | Gauge | STABLE | Healthy pod count |
| `kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total` [38] | Counter | STABLE | Container restart count |
| `kube_pod_status_phase` [38] | Gauge | STABLE | Pod lifecycle state |

Kubernetes SLOs provide baseline expectations [39]: API latency ≤1s (mutating, 99th percentile), pod startup ≤5s (stateless, 99th percentile). These are steady-state SLOs, not upgrade-specific.

OpenShift PDBForceDrainTimeout: 60 minutes, then PDBs are overridden (Tier 2). K8s 1.26+ `unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow` recommended for upgrades [40] [41].

**Critical counter-evidence:** PDBs only protect against eviction API calls, not direct deletes or controller-initiated changes [36]. Restart count is cumulative, never resets, and requires rate-based alerting (`increase(...[1h])`) rather than absolute thresholds. Pod "ready" doesn't guarantee correct application state.

See [references/stateful-workload-continuity.md](references/stateful-workload-continuity.md) for full details.

## 6. Version Skip Validation

**Summary:** Kubernetes enforces sequential minor version upgrades for the control plane. Kubelet skew expanded to N-3 in v1.25 [48]. OpenShift EUS provides verified EUS-to-EUS upgrade paths but still requires traversing intermediate versions [44]. KEP-4330 enables future skip-level upgrades [45].

| Component | Allowed Skew | Source |
|---|---|---|
| kubelet → apiserver | N-3 (N-2 pre-1.25) [42] | K8s version skew policy |
| controller-manager → apiserver | N-1 [42] | K8s version skew policy |
| kubectl → apiserver | ±1 [42] | K8s version skew policy |
| OpenShift EUS | Sequential through intermediates [44] | EUS enhancement |
| GKE Distributed Cloud nodes | Skip allowed (v1.29+) [46] | GKE docs |
| OLM operators | Via skipRange/skips [63] | OLM docs |

70% of reschedulable pods are moved more than necessary during sequential OpenShift upgrades — the EUS worker MCP pause optimization addresses this [44].

**Critical counter-evidence:** Version skip testing is combinatorially impractical for ISVs. Most test only the last 3 versions of 1 distribution. Double-jump upgrades work in practice despite no official support [47]. Google GKE Distributed Cloud officially supports node pool skipping [46].

See [references/version-skip-validation.md](references/version-skip-validation.md) for full details.

## 7. API Compatibility Regression

**Summary:** The Kubernetes deprecation policy provides the most precise guarantees: GA APIs are indefinite within major version, Beta APIs get ~18 months [49]. The `apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis` Prometheus metric (STABLE) enables monitoring [49] [50]. Three scanning tools (Pluto [51], Kubent [52], Kubepug [53]) enable pre-upgrade detection.

| Guarantee | Timeline | Source |
|---|---|---|
| GA API lifetime | Indefinite within major version [49] | K8s deprecation policy |
| Beta API total support | ~18 months (9+9) [49] | K8s deprecation policy |
| Alpha API | None — removable any release [49] | K8s deprecation policy |
| Deprecation → removal | 2-3 years typical [54] | K8s migration guide |
| API endpoint test coverage | 11% (2018) → ~94% (v1.25) [15] | CNCF blog |

**Critical counter-evidence:** Conformance tests cover only ~5-6% of the e2e suite [12] [16]. Static analysis tools miss runtime behavioral changes. API field behavior can change without version change. Objects stored in etcd using removed APIs become read-only [55].

See [references/api-compatibility-regression.md](references/api-compatibility-regression.md) for full details.

## 8. Operator Lifecycle Upgrade Mechanics

**Summary:** OLM exposes `csv_succeeded` (binary 0/1) and `csv_abnormal` (with phase/reason labels) as Prometheus metrics [59]. OpenShift's managed upgrade operator provides 7 upgrade-specific metrics [68]. However, CSV Succeeded doesn't guarantee operator health [64], and the scorecard "does not run your operator" [17].

| Metric | Type | What It Measures |
|---|---|---|
| `csv_succeeded` (csv_up) [59] | Gauge 0/1 | CSV in Succeeded phase |
| `csv_abnormal` [59] | Gauge | Non-succeeded CSVs with reason |
| `csv_sync_total` [60] | Counter | Sync operations (~15-450 series/CSV) |
| `controller_runtime_reconcile_total` [67] | Counter | Reconciliation outcomes |
| 7 managed upgrade operator metrics [68] | Counters/Gauges | Validation, health, timeout failures |

Operator capability Level 2 (Seamless Upgrades) required for Red Hat certification of CNI operators [62]. Requirements: non-disruptive upgrades, backward compatibility, status reporting [61].

**Critical counter-evidence:** CSV Succeeded with only 1 of 2 required pods — confirmed bug [64]. OLM v1 created because v0 architecture was "inadequate" after "five years of real-world use" [65]. Failed install blocks all operators in the namespace [65]. CRD validation had bugs producing both false positives and false negatives (OCPBUGS-46054, OCPBUGS-35373).

See [references/operator-lifecycle-upgrade.md](references/operator-lifecycle-upgrade.md) for full details.

## Cross-Cutting Patterns

### What's Common Across Dimensions

1. **Binary gates dominate over continuous metrics.** CNCF conformance (100% or fail), CSV phase (Succeeded or not), version skew (compliant or not). Continuous numeric metrics exist for data integrity and workload continuity but lack ecosystem-wide thresholds.

2. **Vendor-measurable ≠ operator-measurable.** OpenShift CI runs Fisher's Exact test across thousands of jobs [14]. An operator can run Sonobuoy conformance but cannot replicate the vendor's statistical regression detection.

3. **Counter-perspectives are structurally sound.** Every dimension has documented cases where the primary metric failed to detect real problems: etcd silent corruption [8], conformance tests passing while clusters break [19], CSV Succeeded with unhealthy pods [64], PDBs bypassed during upgrades.

4. **No upgrade-specific SLOs exist.** Kubernetes SLOs cover steady-state operations [39]. No platform publishes upgrade-specific latency, availability, or duration SLOs.

### Practical Measurement Framework

What an operator can actually measure today, ordered by implementation difficulty:

**Tier 1 — Available out of the box (Prometheus + kube-state-metrics):**
- `kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total` — restart rate during upgrade window [38]
- `kube_poddisruptionbudget_status_pod_disruptions_allowed` — PDB blocking [37]
- `kube_pod_status_phase` — pod health distribution [38]
- `apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis` — deprecated API usage [49]
- `csv_succeeded` / `csv_abnormal` — operator upgrade health [59]

**Tier 2 — Requires tooling setup:**
- Sonobuoy conformance tests (pre/post upgrade) [13]
- Pluto/Kubent/Kubepug deprecated API scans [51] [52] [53]
- Flagger/Argo Rollouts canary analysis (application-level) [31] [34]
- DORA Change Failure Rate tracking [30]

**Tier 3 — Requires organizational process:**
- Upgrade duration tracking (no automated metric; manual measurement against formula [20])
- Rollback success tracking (no ecosystem metric; tracked via DORA FDRT [30])
- Version skip compliance (manual verification against skew policy [42])

## Gaps and Limitations

1. **No industry standard for post-upgrade test coverage percentage.** All sources describe risk-based testing rather than percentage targets.
2. **No P95/P99 upgrade duration SLOs anywhere.** Environmental variation (7-15x between cloud and bare metal) makes universal targets impractical.
3. **Rollback success rate is structurally unmeasurable** at the platform level because most platforms don't support rollback at all.
4. **CSV Succeeded is an unreliable health signal** — operator health is decoupled from OLM phase tracking [64].
5. **Conformance tests cover only ~5-6% of the e2e suite** [12] [16] — passing conformance does not validate upgrade success.
6. **Pod restart count is a flawed metric** for upgrade validation — cumulative counter with known false-positive issues.
7. **Static API scanning tools miss runtime behavioral changes** — all three tools (Pluto, Kubent, Kubepug) are limited to structural analysis.
8. **Counter-perspectives draw on project issue trackers and vendor advisories** — these are authoritative but inherently biased toward failure cases. The silent majority of successful upgrades are not documented.
